notes.definition: Abiotic factors are the non-living factors in an environment, such as light intensity, temperature and soil pH, that affect the organisms living in a community.
explanation: Every community is affected by the non-living conditions around it. These are called abiotic factors. AQA lists the abiotic factors you need to know as: light intensity; temperature; moisture levels; soil pH and mineral content; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide levels for plants; and oxygen levels for aquatic animals. Each organism can only survive within a certain range of each factor, so a change in an abiotic factor can change which species can live in an area and how many of them there are.

Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature all affect the rate of photosynthesis. If light intensity falls, for example under a thick tree canopy, plants photosynthesise more slowly, make less glucose and grow less. Plants that need a lot of light may disappear, while shade-tolerant plants survive. Because plants are the producers that feed every other organism, a change in light or carbon dioxide can affect the whole food chain.

Temperature affects the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions in all organisms. Most organisms have a range of temperatures in which they can live and reproduce; outside it their enzymes work too slowly, or are denatured if it is too hot. Climate change is shifting temperatures, so some species are moving to cooler places such as higher up mountains or further north.

Moisture levels affect how much water plants can take up through their roots and how fast animals lose water. Few plants grow in very dry soils, and those that do have special adaptations. Soil pH and mineral content control which plants can grow: some plants such as heather grow in acidic soils, while others need neutral or alkaline soil. Plants need mineral ions such as nitrate (for making proteins) and magnesium (for making chlorophyll), so poor soils support fewer plants.

Wind intensity and direction affect plant growth and shape. Strong winds increase the rate of transpiration and water loss, can damage or uproot plants and make trees on exposed hills grow short and bent away from the prevailing wind. Wind direction also affects where seeds and pollen are carried. On coasts, wind carries salt spray that only some plants can tolerate.

For aquatic animals, the oxygen level in the water is an important abiotic factor. Fish and many invertebrates need dissolved oxygen for aerobic respiration. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and pollution by sewage or fertiliser can cause bacteria to use up oxygen. Some invertebrates, such as stonefly larvae, only survive in clean, well-oxygenated water, while others such as rat-tailed maggots and sludge worms survive in water with very little oxygen. Scientists use these species as indicators of pollution.

In exam questions you may be given data about an abiotic factor and the numbers of a species. Describe the pattern using data, then explain it by linking the factor to a process in the organism (photosynthesis, respiration, water loss or enzyme activity) and then to growth, survival or reproduction.
keyFacts: Abiotic factors are non-living factors that affect a community.
AQA abiotic factors: light intensity, temperature, moisture levels, soil pH and mineral content, wind intensity and direction, carbon dioxide levels (plants), oxygen levels (aquatic animals).
Light intensity and carbon dioxide level affect the rate of photosynthesis in plants.
Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it affects growth and survival of all organisms.
Soil pH and mineral content determine which plants can grow in an area.
Strong winds increase water loss from plants and can damage them.
Aquatic animals need dissolved oxygen for respiration; warm or polluted water has less oxygen.
A change in an abiotic factor can change the distribution and population size of species in a community.

keyTerms.definition: A non-living factor in the environment that affects living organisms, for example temperature or soil pH.
A living factor in the environment, such as food availability, predators or pathogens.
The amount of light energy reaching an area; it affects the rate of photosynthesis.
A measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is; it affects which plants can grow there.
Substances such as nitrate and magnesium ions absorbed from the soil by plant roots and needed for healthy growth.
Oxygen gas dissolved in water, needed by aquatic animals for aerobic respiration.
A species whose presence or absence shows the level of an abiotic factor, such as pollution or oxygen level.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a pattern from field data
workedExamples.question: A student measured light intensity and counted the number of daisies at points from an open field into a wood. Light intensity fell from 900 to 100 arbitrary units and the number of daisies fell from 42 to 2 per quadrat. Explain the pattern.
steps: Describe: as light intensity decreases, the number of daisies decreases.
Link to a process: lower light intensity means a lower rate of photosynthesis.
Link to growth: less glucose is made, so daisies grow less and produce fewer flowers and seeds.
Conclude: fewer daisies survive and reproduce in the shade.
workedExamples.answer: Daisy numbers fall as light intensity falls because daisies photosynthesise more slowly in shade, make less glucose for growth and reproduction, and so fewer survive.

workedExamples.title: Comparing oxygen levels in a river
workedExamples.question: Above a sewage outlet, a river has 9 mg/dm³ of dissolved oxygen and many mayfly nymphs. Below the outlet it has 3 mg/dm³ and no mayfly nymphs but many sludge worms. Explain these observations.
steps: Bacteria feed on the sewage and use up dissolved oxygen in respiration, so oxygen falls from 9 to 3 mg/dm³.
Mayfly nymphs need high oxygen levels for aerobic respiration, so they cannot survive below the outlet.
Sludge worms tolerate low oxygen, so they survive and have less competition.
workedExamples.answer: The sewage lowers dissolved oxygen; mayfly nymphs need a lot of oxygen so they die out, but sludge worms can survive low oxygen and thrive.

workedExamples.title: Reading values from a table
workedExamples.question: Heather cover was 60% in soil of pH 4.5 and 5% in soil of pH 7.0. Calculate how many times greater the cover was at pH 4.5 and suggest what this tells you.
steps: Heather cover is 12 times greater at pH 4.5.
pH 4.5 is acidic, pH 7.0 is neutral.
workedExamples.answer: 12 times greater. Heather grows best in acidic soil; soil pH is an abiotic factor affecting its distribution.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think food availability and predators are abiotic factors.
misconceptions.right: In fact these are biotic factors because they involve living organisms. Abiotic factors are non-living, such as light, temperature, water and pH.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think oxygen level is an important abiotic factor for land plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact AQA links oxygen levels to aquatic animals, which rely on dissolved oxygen. Carbon dioxide level is the gas factor linked to plants.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think higher temperature always means more growth.
misconceptions.right: In fact each organism has an optimum; above it enzymes denature and below it reactions are slow, so growth falls outside the best range.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think warm water holds more oxygen because it is more active.
misconceptions.right: In fact warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water, so fish may struggle in warm or still water.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write 'it affects the plant' without explaining how.
misconceptions.right: In fact you need to link the factor to a process (photosynthesis, enzyme activity, water loss, respiration) and then to growth, survival or reproduction.

realWorld: Freshwater invertebrates such as stonefly nymphs and sludge worms are used by the Environment Agency as indicator species to monitor oxygen levels and pollution in rivers.
Gardeners test soil pH before choosing plants: rhododendrons and heathers need acidic soil, while lavender prefers alkaline soil.
Trees on exposed coasts and hilltops grow short and bent in the direction of the prevailing wind, and farmers plant hedges as windbreaks to protect crops.
examTips: Learn the AQA list of abiotic factors exactly. If asked to name abiotic factors, avoid giving living factors such as predators or food.
When explaining the effect of a change, use a chain: factor changes, process in organism changes (photosynthesis, enzymes, water loss, respiration), growth or survival changes, population changes.
When describing data, quote numbers with units from the table or graph, for example 'as light intensity fell from 900 to 100 au, daisies fell from 42 to 2 per quadrat'.
Correlation is not proof: when two factors change along a transect, say that other factors (such as moisture or pH) may also have changed.
summary: Abiotic factors are non-living factors that affect communities.
AQA factors: light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH and minerals, wind, CO₂ (plants), O₂ (aquatic animals).
Light and CO₂ affect photosynthesis, so they affect producers and therefore whole food chains.
Temperature affects enzymes in all organisms.
Soil pH, minerals and moisture decide which plants can grow in an area.
Dissolved oxygen limits which animals live in water; pollution can lower it.

flashcards.back: A non-living factor in the environment that affects a community.

flashcards.front: List the seven abiotic factors named by AQA.
flashcards.back: Light intensity; temperature; moisture levels; soil pH and mineral content; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide levels for plants; oxygen levels for aquatic animals.

flashcards.front: Why does light intensity affect plants?
flashcards.back: It affects the rate of photosynthesis, so how much glucose is made for growth.

flashcards.front: Which abiotic factor is especially important for aquatic animals?
flashcards.back: Oxygen level (dissolved oxygen) in the water.

flashcards.front: Which gas level is an abiotic factor for plants?

flashcards.back: It affects the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions; too hot denatures enzymes, too cold slows reactions.

flashcards.front: How can strong wind affect plants?
flashcards.back: It increases water loss by transpiration, can damage or uproot plants, and spreads seeds and pollen in the wind direction.

flashcards.front: Why is soil mineral content important?
flashcards.back: Plants need mineral ions such as nitrate (for proteins) and magnesium (for chlorophyll) to grow.

flashcards.front: Why does warm water often contain fewer fish?
flashcards.back: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, so there is less for aerobic respiration.

flashcards.front: How can sewage pollution lower oxygen in a river?
flashcards.back: Bacteria feeding on the sewage respire and use up the dissolved oxygen.

flashcards.front: Give an example of an indicator species for low oxygen in water.
flashcards.back: Sludge worms or rat-tailed maggots (they survive low oxygen).

flashcards.front: Is 'number of predators' abiotic or biotic?

questions.question: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
markScheme: 1 mark: soil pH
questions.explanation: Soil pH is non-living, so it is abiotic. Predators, food and pathogens are all living (biotic) factors.

questions.question: Which abiotic factor directly affects whether aquatic animals can survive in a river?
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen level
questions.explanation: Aquatic animals need dissolved oxygen for respiration, and the amount in water varies a lot. Wind and soil minerals mainly affect land plants.

questions.question: Which list contains only abiotic factors?
options: Pathogens, soil pH, carbon dioxide level
Food availability, oxygen level, wind direction
markScheme: 1 mark: moisture level, wind intensity, temperature
questions.explanation: Moisture, wind and temperature are all non-living. Each other option includes one biotic factor: predators, pathogens or food availability.

questions.question: Which gas level is an abiotic factor that affects the growth of plants?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Plants need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, so its concentration affects their growth. Nitrogen gas cannot be used directly by plants.

questions.question: Why do few plants grow on the floor of a dense forest?
options: The soil contains too much oxygen
Temperature is too high for enzymes
There is too much carbon dioxide
markScheme: 1 mark: low light intensity limits photosynthesis
questions.explanation: The canopy absorbs most of the light, so plants on the floor cannot photosynthesise fast enough to grow well. Forest floors are usually cool, and extra carbon dioxide would help, not harm, photosynthesis.

questions.question: Why does warm, still water often support fewer fish than cold, fast-flowing water?
options: Warm water contains less dissolved oxygen
Warm water contains more dissolved oxygen
Fish cannot respire in warm water
Warm water has a lower pH
markScheme: 1 mark: warm water contains less dissolved oxygen
questions.explanation: Gases are less soluble in warm water, and still water mixes less with air, so oxygen is lower. Fish can still respire in warm water but have less oxygen available.

questions.question: Trees on a windy hilltop are often short with branches growing mostly on one side. Which abiotic factor best explains their shape?
markScheme: 1 mark: wind intensity and direction
questions.explanation: Strong winds from one direction damage buds and dry out shoots on the exposed side, so growth occurs mainly on the sheltered side.

questions.question: A field has poor growth of grass with yellow leaves. Soil tests show low levels of magnesium ions. Which explanation is correct?
options: Magnesium is needed to make proteins, so the grass cannot grow
Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll, so less light is absorbed for photosynthesis
Magnesium is needed for the cell wall, so cells burst
Magnesium lowers soil pH, so roots cannot absorb water
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll, so less light is absorbed for photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Mineral content of soil is an abiotic factor. Without magnesium plants make less chlorophyll, so leaves turn yellow and photosynthesise less. Nitrate, not magnesium, is needed for proteins.

questions.question:
A student placed quadrats every 2 m along a transect from the edge of a pond up a slope.
Table 1 shows the results.
Which factor is the most likely cause of the distribution of rushes?
markScheme: 1 mark: moisture level of the soil
questions.explanation: Table 1 shows light intensity is almost the same along the whole transect, so it cannot explain the pattern. Soil moisture falls steeply moving away from the pond, and the number of rushes falls with it, so moisture is the likely abiotic cause. Carbon dioxide in air barely varies over a few metres, and herbivores are biotic.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about two sites close to each other.
Which abiotic factor is most likely to explain the distribution of heather?

headers: Mean number of heather plants per m²

markScheme: 1 mark: soil pH
questions.explanation: Table 1 shows the only factor given that differs is soil pH: the moorland soil is acidic and the chalk soil is alkaline. Heather is adapted to acidic soils, so soil pH controls where it grows.

questions.question: Name three abiotic factors that can affect a community of plants.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three from: light intensity; temperature; moisture level; soil pH; soil mineral content; wind intensity or direction; carbon dioxide level
questions.explanation: Any three from the AQA list earn the marks. Do not give biotic factors such as herbivores or disease.

questions.question: What is meant by an abiotic factor?
markScheme: 1 mark: non-living
questions.explanation: Abiotic means non-living. Biotic means living.

questions.question: Explain why an increase in carbon dioxide level might increase the growth of plants in a greenhouse.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis / rate of photosynthesis increases (if CO₂ is limiting)
1 mark: more glucose made for growth (e.g. for respiration or making cellulose and proteins)
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a reactant in photosynthesis. More of it can raise the rate, giving more glucose to use for growth.

questions.question: Explain why a very low temperature reduces the growth of plants.
markScheme: 1 mark: enzyme-controlled reactions (such as photosynthesis and respiration) are slower
1 mark: so less glucose is made or used for growth
questions.explanation: At low temperatures molecules move more slowly and there are fewer successful collisions between enzymes and substrates, so photosynthesis and growth slow down.

questions.question: Explain how strong winds can affect the water balance of a plant.
markScheme: 1 mark: wind increases the rate of transpiration / evaporation from leaves
1 mark: so the plant loses more water and may wilt if it cannot replace it
questions.explanation: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient, so water evaporates and diffuses out faster.

questions.question:
Untreated sewage enters a river.
Figure 1 shows the concentration of dissolved oxygen in the river at different distances downstream of the sewage pipe.
The number of fish falls sharply between 1 km and 3 km downstream.
Explain why.

The student concluded that an increase in soil moisture causes an increase in the number of moss plants.
Evaluate the student's conclusion.

markScheme: 1 mark: the data show a positive correlation between moisture and moss number
1 mark: but correlation does not prove causation / other abiotic factors (for example light intensity, soil pH, temperature) may also change along the transect
1 mark: suggestion to measure other factors or repeat transects / carry out a controlled experiment
questions.explanation: Field data usually show correlations. To claim moisture is the cause you need to rule out other factors that change in the same direction.

questions.question: Name one mineral ion that plants absorb from the soil.
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrate or magnesium (allow phosphate or potassium)
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions are used to make proteins and magnesium ions to make chlorophyll. Soil mineral content is an abiotic factor.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the concentration of dissolved oxygen in a river above and below a sewage pipe.
Calculate the decrease in dissolved oxygen.
markScheme: 1 mark: 6.8 mg/dm³
questions.explanation: 10.2 − 3.4 = 6.8 mg/dm³. This drop in oxygen is caused by bacteria respiring as they feed on the sewage.

questions.question:
A student counted bluebells in quadrats in two areas of a wood.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage decrease in the mean number of bluebells per quadrat under the holly bushes compared with the open clearing.

headers: Mean number of bluebells per quadrat

questions.explanation: 48 − 18 = 30; 30 ÷ 48 = 0.625; × 100 = 62.5%. Holly is evergreen, so light intensity is low under it all year.

questions.question:
A student measured the light intensity at five points under a tree.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean light intensity.
markScheme: 1 mark: 128 lux
questions.explanation: Add the readings: 640. Divide by the number of readings, 5, to get 128 lux. Light meters are used to measure this abiotic factor in fieldwork.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the maximum mass of oxygen that can dissolve in fresh water at different temperatures.
Calculate the percentage decrease in dissolved oxygen when water warms from 10 °C to 30 °C.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: 33%
questions.explanation: 11.3 − 7.6 = 3.7; 3.7 ÷ 11.3 = 0.327; × 100 = 32.7%, or 33% to 2 significant figures. Less oxygen in warm water can limit aquatic animals.

questions.question:
A student wants to measure one abiotic factor in a field.
Name one piece of equipment the student could use and the abiotic factor it measures.
markScheme: 1 mark: named equipment (for example light meter, thermometer or temperature probe, pH probe or indicator kit, moisture meter, anemometer)
1 mark: matching factor (light intensity, temperature, soil pH, moisture, wind speed)
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors can be measured directly. The equipment must match the factor, for example a light meter for light intensity.

questions.question:
A student sampled the invertebrates in a river above and below a farm.
Table 1 shows the results.
What does this most likely indicate about the water downstream of the farm?
options: It has a higher oxygen level
It is colder and faster flowing
It has a lower oxygen level, possibly from fertiliser or slurry pollution
It has more light, so more plants grow
markScheme: 1 mark: it has a lower oxygen level, possibly from fertiliser or slurry pollution
questions.explanation: Stonefly and mayfly nymphs need well-oxygenated water; rat-tailed maggots can breathe air through a tube and survive very low oxygen. The change of species indicates lower oxygen downstream, possibly from fertiliser or slurry pollution.

questions.question: Give one reason why few plants grow in very dry soil.
markScheme: 1 mark: not enough water for photosynthesis or to keep cells turgid / plants wilt (allow: mineral ions are absorbed dissolved in water)
questions.explanation: Moisture level is an abiotic factor. Water is needed for photosynthesis, for support, and to carry mineral ions into the roots.

questions.question: A large tree is cut down in a woodland. Describe and explain how the abiotic factors on the woodland floor beneath it might change, and how this could affect the plants growing there.
markScheme: Indicative content: light intensity increases; so rate of photosynthesis increases for ground plants; more glucose so faster growth; light-loving species can now grow; temperature may increase in the day; soil moisture may fall as more evaporation and more wind; or may rise as the tree no longer takes up water; wind intensity increases; species that need shade or moisture may decline.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes at least two abiotic changes and explains their effects on plants using processes such as photosynthesis or water loss.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states one or two changes with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The main change is more light, which increases photosynthesis. Good answers also consider temperature, moisture and wind, and how different species respond.

questions.question:
Climate change is causing ocean temperatures to rise. Some fish species are moving to cooler, deeper water or further from the equator.
Explain how a rise in water temperature could affect fish and the communities they live in.
markScheme: Indicative content: warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen; less oxygen for aerobic respiration in fish; fish may be less active or die; temperature affects enzyme activity in fish; above optimum enzymes may denature, so metabolism and growth are affected; fish move to cooler water where conditions suit them; species that cannot move may decline; changes to fish numbers affect predators (seabirds, seals) that eat them; prey of the fish (smaller fish, invertebrates) may increase; new species may move in and compete; coral may be damaged, removing habitats; community composition changes.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed explanation linking temperature to both oxygen solubility and enzyme activity, and clear consequences for distribution and for other organisms in the community.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains at least one physiological effect and one effect on distribution or other species.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example fish move away or die, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Two abiotic links are expected: less dissolved oxygen in warm water, and the effect of temperature on enzymes. Then follow the change through the community via predators, prey and competitors.

markScheme: Indicative content: the dune top is more exposed to strong wind; wind increases water loss by transpiration; sand drains quickly so moisture level is low; few mineral ions in loose sand; salt spray from the sea; only plants adapted to dry, windy, salty conditions survive (for example marram grass); the hollow is sheltered, moister and has more organic matter and mineral ions; so a wider range of plants can grow there and compete.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): compares two or more abiotic factors between the sites and links them to which plants can survive.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one or two factors that differ without clear explanation.
questions.explanation: Compare wind, moisture and mineral content between the two sites, and link each to survival. Only adapted plants survive the harsher conditions on the dune top.
